Washoe County by the numbers

What is Washoe County and how is it laid out?

Washoe County is in the northwest corner of Nevada, and Reno is its county seat. It covers 6,542 square miles, of which 6,302 are land, and its 2020 census population was 486,492, which makes it the second most populous county in the state.

Only two cities are incorporated here, Reno and Sparks. The rest of the county is made up of unincorporated communities. The Wikipedia article on the county lists Cold Springs, Crystal Bay, Empire, Gerlach, Golden Valley, Incline Village, Lemmon Valley, Mogul, Nixon, Spanish Springs, Sun Valley, Sutcliffe, Verdi, Wadsworth and Washoe Valley as census-designated places. The highest point is Mount Rose at 10,785 feet, and Pyramid Lake lies in the north.

That layout matters for property tax. A house in Incline Village, one in Sun Valley and one in downtown Reno are all billed by the same Treasurer, and the Assessor publishes tax district maps and neighborhood maps for the county.

How did Washoe County come about?

Washoe County was created on November 25, 1861, as one of the nine original counties of Nevada Territory, and it is named after the Washoe people. It was consolidated with Roop County in 1864. Washoe City was the first county seat, and Reno replaced it in 1871.

The Truckee Meadows drew settlers in the 1850s, and the Junction House was established south of the Truckee River in 1850. Pyramid Lake was named by Lieutenant John C. Fremont in January 1844. A 2010 ballot question asked whether the Reno and Washoe County governments should consolidate; unofficial results showed 54 percent of voters approving it.

What drives the Washoe County economy?

Washoe County mixes tourism, logistics, manufacturing and technology. Between 2020 and 2025 the number of jobs in the county rose 13.1 percent, compared with 10.6 percent nationally. In the Lake Tahoe Basin, more than 40 percent of jobs were related to tourism in 2013.

The county school district, the University of Nevada, Reno, Renown Regional Medical Center and several large casinos are the biggest employers in Reno. Sierra Nevada Corporation is based in Sparks, and the Tesla Gigafactory at the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center, just outside Washoe in Storey County, employs about 11,000 people.

For an owner thinking about selling, the county's own statistics are worth knowing. The Assessor posts Sales Reports, a Median Sales Chart and Current Statistical Reports on its online data pages, so you can see recorded sale prices for your area before you compare them with an offer.

What hazards should Washoe County sellers watch?

The county is wildfire prone, and most of that risk is in southern Reno and just outside the city limits. Many fires in southwest Reno have spread quickly, including the Caughlin Fire in 2011. Structures are also being built in forested areas.

The Assessor's office answers questions about whether a property is within a FEMA floodplain and can provide elevation certificates. Both questions come up when a buyer's lender or insurer asks.

  • Disclose known fire damage, burn scars or smoke damage on the Nevada disclosure form
  • Ask the Assessor for the floodplain status of the parcel
  • Check whether unpermitted additions need a Washoe County Building review

Who bills and who values property in Washoe County?

Washoe County divides the work between three offices, and sellers deal with each at a different stage. The Assessor values the property and handles appeals and exemptions, the Treasurer bills and collects tax, and the Recorder records the deed and collects the real property transfer tax.

OfficeWhat it doesContact
AssessorValues, tax cap status, exemptions, Board of Equalization appeals(775) 328-2277
TreasurerBills, collections, delinquent parcels, online payments775.328.2510, tax@washoecounty.gov, 1001 E 9th Street, Room D140, Reno
RecorderRecording deeds, Declaration of Value, transfer tax(775) 328-3661 for transfer tax questions

The Treasurer cannot take payments by telephone, so pay online or by mail. Customer service runs Monday through Friday, 8am to 5pm.

What deadlines matter for a Washoe County property tax year?

The county fiscal year runs from July 1 through June 30, with July 1 as the lien date. These are the dates the Assessor lists, besides the installment dates already shown above.

  • December 18: value notices mailed to owners
  • January 1: the real property roll closes
  • January 15: deadline to appeal to the County Board of Equalization
  • March 10: deadline to appeal a County Board decision to the State Board
  • June 15: deadline to renew or apply for most exemptions, and for rental owners to file the tax cap form for the next fiscal year
  • June 30: deadline to appeal a tax cap determination for the current year
  • July 5: deadline to apply for an exemption on property acquired after June 15 and before July 1

If January 15 falls on a weekend or holiday, the appeal may be filed on the next business day.

How does the 3 percent tax cap work when a house sells?

The tax cap limits the growth of the tax bill, not the assessed value. Under Assembly Bill 489, signed in 2005, a primary residence has a 3 percent cap on its bill, and other property has a higher cap. Some rental dwellings may also qualify for 3 percent. The only property with no cap is property new to the roll, such as new construction, new parcels or a parcel with a change in use.

Washoe County mails an affidavit to residential rental owners in early May that must be returned by June 15, and it sends affidavits to non-rental properties after a change in ownership. Until a qualifying affidavit is filed, the property sits at the higher general abatement. The Assessor has 30 days to answer an appeal of a tax cap decision. The Assessor's phone number is (775) 328-2277.

A buyer of a primary residence who files promptly can have the 3 percent cap applied, while an investor buying a rental may see a different cap. Telling a buyer this early can head off a surprise on the first bill.

What happens to the tax bill at closing?

Taxes for the fiscal year are a lien from July 1, and the Washoe County Treasurer will advertise parcels that are delinquent. Owners have 2 years from the date the lien is filed to redeem by paying all taxes, penalties and costs. Penalties follow NRS 361.483, and the county billing page gives no percentages.

One detail often missed: the supplemental tax bill is not sent to the mortgage company. A seller who is paying off a loan should check whether a supplemental bill was issued for a recent improvement or new construction.

Real property transfer tax is separate. The Washoe County rate is $2.05 per $500 of value, which is the $1.95 statewide rate plus $0.10. On a $500,000 sale that is $2,050. The Recorder collects it when the deed is recorded, using the Declaration of Value, and the base is either the price or the estimated fair market value, which uses the assessor's taxable value or a prior purchase price within five years, whichever is higher. Exemptions under NRS 375.090 include transfers between former spouses under a divorce decree and transfers into a trust without consideration.

Can you sell a Washoe County house for cash when taxes are owed?

Yes. Owing property tax does not by itself stop a sale, but the unpaid amount has to be dealt with in the deal. We buy Washoe County houses as-is, including houses behind on taxes, inherited houses and rentals. We give a written offer and you owe nothing if you decline.

Before you sell, request the tax balance from the Treasurer, check your tax cap status with the Assessor and ask the Recorder about the Declaration of Value. NRS 113.130 still requires a disclosure form at least 10 days before conveyance.

More questions about Washoe County, NV Property Tax Guide

Who collects property tax in Washoe County?

The Washoe County Treasurer bills and collects it. Bills are mailed by August 1 and taxes are due on the third Monday in August, with installments allowed when a parcel's tax exceeds $100. Payments cannot be taken over the phone.

When do I have to appeal my Washoe County assessment?

Appeals to the County Board of Equalization are due by January 15, or the next business day if that falls on a weekend or holiday. You can appeal a County Board decision to the State Board of Equalization by March 10.

What is the Washoe County transfer tax rate?

It is $2.05 per $500 of value, made up of the $1.95 statewide rate plus $0.10 for Washoe County. The Recorder collects it when the deed is recorded. A $500,000 sale carries $2,050.

How does the 3 percent tax cap apply to a new buyer?

The cap applies to the tax bill of a primary residence. After a change in ownership the Assessor mails an affidavit, and the property stays at the higher cap until a qualifying affidavit is returned.

How long do I have to redeem a delinquent Washoe County parcel?

Owners have two years from the date the lien is filed to redeem by paying all taxes, delinquencies and costs. Delinquent properties are advertised in the local newspaper.

Does a supplemental tax bill go to my mortgage company?

No. The Washoe County Treasurer says the supplemental bill is not sent to the mortgage company, so the owner should watch for it.

Lyon County by the numbers

Where is Lyon County, Nevada, and what towns does it include?

Lyon County covers 2,024 square miles of western Nevada, about 1.1% of it water, and it is the fourth-smallest Nevada county by area. It borders Carson City on the west, Storey County on the northwest, Churchill County on the east and Mineral County to the southeast.

The county seat is Yerington. The Wikipedia county entry lists these communities:

  • Fernley, Yerington and Dayton
  • Silver Springs and Stagecoach
  • Smith Valley and Mound House

Mound House sits on US 50 right at the line with Carson City, so it is the Lyon County community closest to the state capital.

How did Lyon County get its name and its county seat?

Lyon County was one of the original Nevada counties created on November 25, 1861, and it was named for Nathaniel Lyon, the first Union general killed in the Civil War. Its first county seat was set at Dayton on November 29, 1861. After the Dayton courthouse burned in 1909, the seat moved to Yerington in 1911.

Railroads shaped the county. The Central Pacific, the first transcontinental railroad, ran through it, and the Virginia and Truckee line still passes through Mound House.

What does Lyon County look like by the numbers?

Lyon County had 59,235 residents in the 2020 census, with a median age of 43.0 years. Of 24,401 housing units, 7.0% were vacant, and 74.7% of occupied units were owner-occupied.

About 55.4% of residents lived in urban areas and 44.6% in rural areas, which is a split most Nevada counties do not have.

ItemWhat the source says
CreatedNovember 25, 1861
County seatYerington (moved from Dayton in 1911)
Area2,024 square miles
2020 population59,235
Owner-occupied units (2020)74.7%
Public schools16 schools in the Lyon County School District
Assessment ratio35% of taxable value
Appeal deadlineJanuary 15, or the next business day

What roads and airports serve Lyon County?

The main highways are Interstate 80, US 50, US 95 and US 95 Alternate, with Interstate 11 shown as a future route. Business Loop I-80 connects Wadsworth and Fernley.

The county has the Yerington Municipal Airport with a 5,800-foot runway and the Silver Springs Airport with a 6,000-foot runway. Tiger Field, near Fernley on US 95A, has a gravel runway and a paved one of 5,600 feet. The Union Pacific line still serves the NV Energy Fort Churchill Generating Station near Yerington.

Utilities come from NV Energy for electric service and Southwest Gas for natural gas. The county's own building FAQ notes that power is not approved on vacant parcels, which can matter if you are selling raw land.

Who handles property tax in Lyon County?

Three offices split the work. The Assessor values property, the Clerk-Treasurer bills and collects, and the Nevada Tax Commission sets the rate each spring from budgets submitted by local entities. The Assessor's phone number is 775-463-6520. The Clerk-Treasurer is at 27 S Main Street in Yerington and takes calls at 775-463-6501.

The Assessor's FAQ says the office does not set the rate or collect taxes. Its duty is to find taxable property, appraise it, and calculate 35% of that appraised value as the assessed value. Land is appraised by market value for its use. Buildings are priced at replacement cost new, then depreciated at 1.5% per year, to a maximum of 75%.

The county says market value has very little bearing on taxable value, especially as improvements get older. Values can change every year, through reappraisal or through factors approved by the Tax Commission. Assessment notices go out in December and June to owners whose value changed.

When is Lyon County property tax due and how do I pay it?

Real property tax is billed once a year and paid in four installments. Under NRS 361.483, the first is due on the third Monday of August, the second on the first Monday of October, the third on the first Monday of January and the fourth on the first Monday of March.

The county's practical points are worth knowing before a sale:

  • Bills are mailed in mid to late July, since the fiscal year runs July 1 to June 30.
  • One bill is mailed to the address on file, or to the servicer if the county has been told one pays the tax.
  • The county does not send a bill at each installment, and sends no reminders or payment confirmations.
  • Not receiving a bill does not excuse late payment. If it has not come by early August, call the office for a reprint.
  • There is a 10-day grace period after each due date.

You can pay online by scanning the QR code on the bill or searching the parcel on the county portal, by phone, in person at 27 S Main Street, by check in the drop box (not cash), or by mail to the Lyon County Treasurer. Penalties of 4% for one late installment up to 7% for four follow state law.

How do I appeal a Lyon County assessment?

Talk to the Assessor first, then file with the County Board of Equalization by January 15. If January 15 falls on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day.

The county's order of appeal runs as follows:

  1. Call or visit the Assessor's Office to discuss the value with an appraiser.
  2. File the appeal with the Assessor's Office by the January 15 deadline.
  3. If still unsatisfied, appeal to the State Board of Equalization.
  4. After that, the court system.

Any of these bodies may adjust the assessed value. The Assessor's office cannot change a tax rate. The County Board of Equalization has held its appeal hearings in February, and its published agendas list each appeal.

What does the Lyon County Recorder require when a house sells?

Every transfer of title needs a Declaration of Value form so the Recorder can decide whether transfer tax is due or an exemption applies. The form goes with deeds, contracts of sale and some court orders. The Recorder's phone is 775-463-6581, and copies of a recorded deed can be requested online, by phone or in person with advance payment.

Nevada's statewide Real Property Transfer Tax is $1.95 per $500 of value, with extra amounts only in Washoe, Churchill and Clark counties. Lyon County is not on that list. Buyer and seller are both liable, and the tax is collected when the deed is recorded. Exemptions include transfers to or from a trust without consideration and a deed upon death under NRS 111.109.

The Recorder also keeps lien records, so a document search shows what is recorded against a property. Owners can record a Declaration of Homestead, which gives protection from involuntary liens. If a death certificate is needed for an inherited house, it comes from vital statistics in the state where the death occurred, not from the county.

What building and permit issues come up when selling in Lyon County?

Unpermitted work is the item that most often slows a Lyon County sale. The county's building FAQ sets these rules:

  • A detached shed under 200 square feet with no electrical, mechanical or plumbing needs no permit. Larger ones, or ones with utilities, do.
  • Decks attached to a building need a permit. Detached decks under 200 square feet and less than 30 inches high do not, but must still meet code.
  • Fences of seven feet or less need no permit. Front yard fences are limited to 3 feet.
  • A permit becomes invalid if work does not start within 180 days or stops for 180 days.
  • A residential permit's final signed inspection serves as the certificate of occupancy.

Manufactured homes get extra scrutiny. They are allowed in most residential districts if no more than 6 years old when moved, certified under the 1974 federal standard, and at least 1,200 square feet in more than one section. The county warns that non-permitted additions or modifications can impair future financing and sale. A failed septic leach field must be replaced under a county permit, and in the Mason and Smith valleys the Walker River Irrigation District must approve site plans.

What should a Lyon County seller with tax due do first?

Get the exact balance and the dates, then decide how quickly you need to close. Cash Home Buyers purchases houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to the seller, and the title company pays unpaid tax out of proceeds. Confirm every deadline, rate and fee with the Lyon County Assessor, Clerk-Treasurer and Recorder, since official pages change each fiscal year.

More questions about Lyon County, NV Property Tax Guide

Where do I pay property tax in Lyon County, Nevada?

The Lyon County Clerk-Treasurer collects it, at 27 S Main Street in Yerington or by phone at 775-463-6501. You can also pay online through the county portal, by mailed check or money order to the Lyon County Treasurer, or in the drop box (checks only).

When are Lyon County property tax installments due?

Under NRS 361.483 they are due on the third Monday of August, the first Monday of October, the first Monday of January and the first Monday of March. A 10-day grace period follows each date.

What is the deadline to appeal a Lyon County property assessment?

January 15, or the first business day after if it falls on a weekend or holiday. File with the Assessor's Office.

Does Lyon County assess property at market value?

No. The Assessor appraises land at market value for its use and buildings at replacement cost new less 1.5% depreciation per year, then takes 35% of that as the assessed value. The county says market value has little bearing on taxable value as buildings age.

Do I owe transfer tax when I sell a house in Lyon County?

Usually yes. The statewide rate is $1.95 per $500 of value, collected by the Recorder when the deed is recorded. Buyer and seller are both responsible, and some transfers are exempt, such as a deed upon death under NRS 111.109.

What if I never got a Lyon County tax bill?

You still owe the tax. NRS 361.480 says failure to receive a bill does not excuse timely payment. Call the Clerk-Treasurer by early August for a reprint.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Who to contact in Carson City County

  • Carson City Treasurer

What we confirmed on official pages

  • Appeal forms available in December until Jan 15; call (775) 887-2130 (from the county site listing; confirm with the office)
  • 10-day grace per installment; late penalties 4%, 5%, 6%, 7% for 1st-4th consecutive late installments; prior-year delinquent taxes accrue interest at 10% APR monthly

Selling in Carson City County?
We buy Carson City County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • Treasurer page lacks payment methods, address, hours
  • Carson City is an independent city/consolidated municipality; its own recorder is separate (not required)

Is Carson City a city or a county?

Carson City is both. It is an independent city and consolidated municipality, treated as a county equivalent, so there is no separate Carson City County government and one set of offices handles both jobs.

Before 1969 the city was the county seat of Ormsby County. That year a referendum approved merging the city and county, and the legislature issued a revised charter that created the Carson City Consolidated Municipality. For property tax this means the City Treasurer, City Assessor and City Recorder do the work a county office does elsewhere in Nevada, which is why people search for a Carson City County tax guide.

The consolidated limits cover about 157 square miles and reach west across the Sierra Nevada to the California-Nevada line in the middle of Lake Tahoe. Most residents live in Eagle Valley on the eastern edge of the Carson Range, roughly 30 miles south of Reno.

What is Carson City's history, and how does it affect homes here?

Carson City was founded in 1858, has been Nevada's capital since 1861, and was incorporated in 1875. It is named for the mountain man Kit Carson and grew from a stopover for California-bound immigrants into a commercial center after the Comstock Lode silver strike nearby.

Nevada became a state in 1864 and Carson City was confirmed as the permanent capital. The Nevada State Capitol was built from 1869 to 1871, and the Virginia and Truckee Railroad ran between Virginia City and Carson City until the tracks were removed in 1950.

That age shows in the housing stock. Older neighborhoods near the Capitol have homes that predate modern codes, and a downtown plan adopted in 1991 limits new buildings within 500 feet of the Capitol so they do not rise above it. Sellers of older houses often face questions about wiring, plumbing and additions built without permits.

What is Carson City's economy and who employs people here?

State government is the foundation. A published list of notable employers for the fourth quarter of 2012 puts the Carson City School District in the 1,000 to 1,499 employee range, with the Nevada Department of Transportation and Western Nevada College at 500 to 999.

The same list places the Nevada Department of Corrections, the Department of Motor Vehicles, Casino Fandango, Walmart, Precision Castparts and the Gold Dust West Hotel and Casino in the 200 to 499 range. The list is more than a decade old, so treat it as a rough picture and not a current ranking.

State agencies and the school district account for several of the largest payrolls on that list.

How do the climate and roads affect a Carson City house?

Carson City has a cold semi-arid climate in a high desert river valley, about 4,802 feet above sea level by the Wikipedia climate summary. Winters bring light to moderate snow, averaging 14.0 inches, and most precipitation falls in winter and spring.

The snow total is modest next to the mountain towns, but the range is wide: the snowiest season on record was 82.1 inches in 1951 to 1952, and the least was 3.1 inches in 2002 to 2003. Roofs, pipes and heating should be ready for a heavy year.

Four highways serve the city: Nevada State Route 28, U.S. 395, U.S. 50 and Interstate 580, its only freeway. The Carson City Freeway project finished its first phase in February 2006.

When are Carson City property taxes due?

Carson City property tax is paid in four installments set by Nevada law: the third Monday in August, and the first Mondays in October, January and March. Each installment has a 10-day grace period.

InstallmentDue date, fiscal year 2026/27
1stMonday, August 17, 2026
2ndMonday, October 5, 2026
3rdMonday, January 4, 2027
4thMonday, March 1, 2027

Bills are mailed each July to the address on file with the Assessor, and they go to the owner even when a lender pays through escrow. The Treasurer, Andrew Rasor, lists the schedule on the city's Treasurer page.

What are the late penalties and the tax sale process in Carson City?

Penalties rise with each consecutive late installment: 4% for the first, 5% for the second, 6% for the third and 7% for the fourth. Prior-year delinquent taxes accrue interest at 10% a year, charged monthly.

Properties with taxes still due at the end of April are advertised as delinquent in the local newspaper. If taxes stay unpaid for three years, the Treasurer takes a trustee deed and can begin a tax sale. The city says only a few parcels have sold in the past fifteen years.

  • A notice cites NRS 361.565 and 361.570.
  • On the first Monday in June the Treasurer issues a certificate holding the property subject to redemption.
  • The owner has two years to redeem by paying taxes, costs and 10% annual interest.

A seller with a delinquent balance should ask for the current payoff before listing, because the figure changes at each installment date.

How do the Carson City tax cap, assessment and appeal dates work?

Nevada limits how fast your bill can rise. Under NRS 361.4723, an owner's primary residence or a qualifying rental gets a 3% cap on the tax bill, while other property gets a higher cap that cannot exceed 8%.

The Carson City Assessor lists the high cap by year, including 6.9% for 2026/27 and 8.0% for each of 2022/23 through 2024/25. The Assessor mails Property Tax Cap Claim forms on April 15 so owner-occupied houses can be told apart from rentals. New construction or a change of use does not get the abatement the first year.

Assessment notices go out in late November, and the key appeal dates are:

  • January 15: last day to petition the County Board of Equalization.
  • January and February: the County Board hears appeals.
  • February and March: the State Board of Equalization meets.
  • June 30, 2027: last day to appeal a tax cap decision for 2026/27.

Appeal forms are available in December through the Assessor's office at (775) 887-2130.

What do recording and transfer tax look like when selling in Carson City?

Every property transfer is taxable, and the Carson City Recorder collects transfer tax at $3.90 per $1,000 of value. The recorder requires a Declaration of Value form with the deed.

That equals $1.95 per $500, which matches the statewide base rate. The Nevada Department of Taxation says the base is $1.95 per $500 in all counties, and that Clark County adds $0.60 on top of it. The Recorder's Office can be reached at (775) 887-2000.

At closing, the title company handles the form, the tax and the proration of the installment in progress. Ask for a written statement before the signing date.

What do sellers in Carson City usually face?

Most sellers here run into timing and paperwork issues.

  • An installment that falls due while the house is in escrow.
  • A tax cap claim that was never filed, or one tied to a rental that has changed use.
  • Older homes with unpermitted work.
  • Inherited property with taxes unpaid for more than one installment.

We buy houses as-is and can work around a tax balance, with the payoff coming from the sale. Whether you list or sell for cash, begin by pulling the parcel's tax status from the Treasurer.

More questions about Carson City County, NV Property Tax Guide

Is there a Carson City County?

Not as a separate government. Carson City is an independent city and consolidated municipality, treated as a county equivalent since the city and Ormsby County merged in 1969.

When are Carson City property taxes due?

In four installments: the third Monday in August and the first Mondays in October, January and March. For fiscal year 2026/27 those are August 17, October 5, January 4 and March 1, each with a 10-day grace period.

What is the Carson City late penalty?

Penalties are 4%, 5%, 6% and 7% for the first through fourth consecutive late installments. Prior-year delinquent taxes accrue interest at 10% a year.

When is the Carson City appeal deadline?

Petitions to appeal a value to the County Board of Equalization are due January 15. The board meets in January and February, and the State Board meets in February and March.

How much is the transfer tax in Carson City?

The Recorder lists transfer tax at $3.90 per $1,000 of value, and a Declaration of Value form is required with the deed.

Can I sell a Carson City house with delinquent taxes?

Yes. The balance is paid from the sale at closing. Taxes unpaid for three years can lead to a trustee deed, so ask the Treasurer for a payoff early.

Clark County by the numbers

How big is Clark County, Nevada, and who lives there?

Clark County is the southernmost and most populous county in Nevada, with 2,265,461 residents at the 2020 census. It holds about 70% of the state's population on only 7% of its land.

The county has 8,061 square miles of land, roughly the size of New Jersey. Las Vegas is the county seat, and Henderson and North Las Vegas are the other two of the state's three largest cities. Boulder City is the largest by area. In all there are five incorporated cities, 21 unincorporated towns and 11 judicial townships.

One detail matters more to sellers than most: more than a million residents live in unincorporated areas that still use a Las Vegas mailing address. Whether your house is inside a city or in an unincorporated town changes which planning, code and utility offices apply, even though the county bills the property tax either way.

What are Clark County's landscape and climate, and how do they affect a house?

Clark County is desert. Greater Las Vegas is a tectonic valley surrounded by four mountain ranges, and the native vegetation is mostly creosote bush outside the forests on Mount Charleston, which reaches 11,918 feet.

The Colorado River forms the southeastern boundary, with Hoover Dam holding back Lake Mead along much of it. The lowest point in Nevada is on the river just south of Laughlin, where it leaves the state.

For a house, desert conditions mean heat on roofs and mechanical systems, strain on air conditioning and attention to landscaping and water use. Wikipedia notes that growth puts strain on the region's water security. We could not confirm a current official figure for average summer highs, so none are stated.

What drives Clark County's economy?

Gaming and tourism are the best-known drivers. The county is home to many gaming-related companies, including MGM Resorts International, Wynn Resorts, Boyd Gaming and Las Vegas Sands.

The Las Vegas Strip, Nellis Air Force Base, Hoover Dam and Harry Reid International Airport are all inside the county. The casino industry is grouped into gaming areas that include the Strip, North Las Vegas, Laughlin, Mesquite and a balance-of-county group that covers places such as Lake Las Vegas, Jean and Primm.

If you need to sell quickly, for a job move or any other reason, check the tax calendar below first, since an installment can fall due while a sale is in progress.

Who handles property tax in Clark County?

The Clark County Assessor values property, the Treasurer bills and collects the tax, and the Recorder records deeds and collects transfer tax. Nevada's Department of Taxation sets the tax rates for each tax district.

  • Treasurer: 500 S Grand Central Pkwy, Box 551220, Las Vegas, NV 89155-1220
  • Treasurer phone: (702) 455-4323; open Monday through Thursday, 7:30 am to 5:30 pm, closed Friday through Sunday
  • Assessor appeals line: (702) 455-4997

The Treasurer mails real property bills only once each fiscal year. If you do not get one by August 1, you can request a copy through the automated phone system, and the county notes that not receiving a bill does not excuse a late payment under NRS 361.480. If you buy during the year or a lender stops paying your taxes, call the office for a bill.

When are Clark County property taxes due, and what are the penalties?

Taxes are due the third Monday in August, but if the total is more than $100 you can pay in installments. The county stresses that these are not quarterly payments.

The installment dates are the third Monday in August and the first Mondays in October, January and March. You must pay within 10 days of the due date to avoid a penalty, and the county's penalty schedule grows with each missed installment:

Installments latePenalty on each late installment
One4%
Two9% on the first, 5% on the second
Three15%, 11% and 6%
Four22%, 18%, 13% and 7%

If a mortgage company holds an escrow account, you should still confirm that it paid on time, because the county says that responsibility is yours. Reminders are available by email or text through the Treasurer's page.

What happens to delinquent property in Clark County?

Properties with unpaid taxes at the end of April are advertised as delinquent in the local newspaper and on the Treasurer's website. If the balance is still unpaid at close of business on the first Monday in June, the Treasurer holds the property for a two-year redemption period.

The owner can redeem by paying the taxes, accruing taxes, penalties and costs, with interest at 10% a year from the original due date. The county tax receiver may shorten the process to one year for property found to be abandoned, under NRS 361.567. If nothing is paid, the property is deeded to the County Treasurer as trustee and can be sold at public auction.

The Treasurer's FAQ says auctions are usually held at least once a year, often in spring, with registration capped at 280 bidders and a $5,000 deposit. The county posted a 2026 auction notice with publication dates in April and May. A property deeded to the trustee after three consecutive delinquent fiscal years, or two if it is abandoned, is subject to auction.

If your house is already on a delinquent list, you can still sell before the redemption period ends, and the payoff comes out of the closing. The county publishes the current rules on its real property tax page.

How does the Clark County Assessor value a home and handle appeals?

The Assessor uses the cost method: replacement cost of the building less depreciation, plus the market value of the land. Depreciation is 1.5% per year of effective age, up to a maximum of 50 years, and values are updated every year.

The county gives a worked example. A new home with a taxable value of $200,000, an assessment ratio of .35 and a rate of 3.2782 per hundred dollars comes to $70,000 of assessed value and a $2,294.74 tax bill for the year. The rate changes by tax district, so your own bill will differ. Homes that already qualify for the 3% or 8% abatement pay the lower of the calculated tax or the capped amount.

  • Appeal forms are available from the Assessor in December.
  • The filing deadline is January 15, or the next business day if it falls on a weekend or holiday.
  • If the County Board of Equalization agrees with the Assessor, you may appeal to the State Board, and then to District Court.

What transfer tax and recording steps apply to a Clark County sale?

The Clark County Recorder charges real property transfer tax at $2.55 per $500 of value or a fraction of it. The tax is based on the full purchase price or the estimated fair market value.

The state explains the pieces: the base rate is $1.95 per $500 in every county, and Clark County adds $0.60. Certain transfers are exempt under NRS 375.090, and the county offers a calculator that gives only an estimate. A Declaration of Value form must go in with the deed, and the Recorder provides it at no charge.

On a $400,000 sale, for example, $2.55 for each $500 works out to 800 units, or $2,040. Your title company will prepare the exact amount, and you can compare it against the county calculator.

What do Clark County sellers usually run into?

The size of the county creates most of the surprises.

  • Tax rates that vary by district, so a neighbor's bill is not a guide to yours.
  • An installment due soon after a sale is signed, with the buyer and seller each owing part of the year.
  • An escrow lender that missed a payment.
  • Inherited property with taxes that went unpaid across several installments.

We buy houses as-is across the county and can close around a tax balance with the payoff coming out of the sale. We do not promise a price before seeing the property. Start by looking up your parcel on the Treasurer's payment site.

More questions about Clark County, NV Property Tax Guide

When are Clark County property taxes due?

The third Monday in August, with installments allowed on the first Mondays in October, January and March if taxes exceed $100. Pay within 10 days of each due date to avoid a penalty.

What is the penalty for paying late in Clark County?

One late installment adds 4%. With two late, the first is charged 9% and the second 5%, and the percentages rise further at three and four late installments.

What is Clark County's transfer tax?

The Recorder charges $2.55 per $500 of value. That is the state base of $1.95 per $500 plus $0.60 added in Clark County.

What is the property tax appeal deadline in Clark County?

Appeals to the County Board of Equalization must be filed by January 15. Forms are available from the Assessor in December, and the number to call is (702) 455-4997.

How long before a delinquent Clark County property can be auctioned?

Unpaid taxes put the property into a two-year redemption period after the first Monday in June. Property deeded to the Treasurer after three consecutive delinquent fiscal years, or two if abandoned, can be auctioned.

Can I sell a Clark County house that has delinquent taxes?

Yes. You can sell before the redemption period ends, and the taxes, penalties and interest are paid out of the proceeds at closing.

Douglas County by the numbers

Where is Douglas County, Nevada, and how is it laid out?

Douglas County sits in far western Nevada, running from the floor of the Carson Valley up into the Sierra Nevada and across the state line at Lake Tahoe. The Census Bureau puts its area at 738 square miles, which makes it the second-smallest county in Nevada by area, and about 13.2% of Lake Tahoe falls inside it.

Carson City, the state capital, lies to the north and Lyon County to the east. The county seat is Minden, which took the title from Genoa in 1915.

There are no incorporated cities or towns in Douglas County. Every community is unincorporated, so the county government handles parks, law enforcement, road maintenance and building inspection for all of them. The Census Bureau tracks these places as census-designated places:

  • Gardnerville and Gardnerville Ranchos
  • Minden (county seat), Genoa, Johnson Lane and Ruhenstroth
  • Indian Hills, Topaz Lake and Topaz Ranch Estates
  • Stateline and Zephyr Cove, on the Lake Tahoe side

That layout matters for a seller because the same two county offices, the Assessor and the Clerk-Treasurer, bill and value a house in Stateline and a house in Gardnerville. There is no city tax office to call.

What is the history of Douglas County, and why does it matter for older homes?

Genoa, in Douglas County, was the first permanent settlement in Nevada. Mormon traders founded it in 1851 to sell goods to settlers heading for California.

The county was named for Stephen A. Douglas and was one of the first nine counties created by the Nevada territorial legislature in 1861. Growth stayed slow for a century. The Census counted 2,029 residents in 1950 and 6,882 in 1970, then 19,421 in 1980 and 41,259 in 2000.

Who lives in Douglas County and who works there?

Douglas County had 49,488 residents in the 2020 census, with a median age of 54.1 years. About 30.7% of residents were 65 or older, and 75.4% of occupied housing units were owner-occupied.

With nearly a third of residents at retirement age, inherited houses and sales by heirs are a natural part of this market, and they inherit the tax calendar along with the deed.

The county's Wikipedia entry lists these among its major employers:

  • The Starbucks roasting plant
  • Patmont Motor Werks
  • Bently Nevada, part of Baker Hughes
  • North Sails
  • TeslaWatt

Douglas County is also part of the Reno-Carson City-Fernley combined statistical area, so many residents commute or work in Carson City and the Reno area. Public schools are run by the Douglas County School District, which serves both the Carson Valley and the Lake Tahoe side.

How does the Douglas County Assessor value a house?

The Assessor sets a taxable value, multiplies it by 35%, and the result is the assessed value that the tax rate is applied to. Taxable value for an improved lot is the land at full cash value for its actual use, plus the replacement cost of the buildings new, less depreciation.

The Nevada Department of Taxation explains that depreciation runs at 1.5% per year of adjusted age, up to a maximum of 50 years. Market price therefore has only an indirect link to the taxable value.

The Assessor's role is valuation only. The county's own page says questions about tax rates or tax amounts belong with locally elected officials, not the Assessor. The combined rate is capped statewide at $3.64 per $100 of assessed value, plus $0.02 for the state debt component, for a total of $3.66.

Two partial abatements limit how fast a bill can rise:

  • Owner-occupied single-family primary residences are held to a 3% increase over the prior year's tax.
  • Other property falls under a general abatement of up to 8%, set by a county-specific formula built on twice the CPI or a nine-year average of assessed value growth.

The abatements do not apply to property with no prior assessed value, property in its first year on the roll after new improvements, or property whose use changes. A house that was recently remodeled or moved from rental to owner-occupied should be checked against those exceptions.

How do I appeal a Douglas County assessment?

Start with a call or visit to the Assessor's office, then file a petition with the County Board of Equalization by January 15. The county says most questions are settled at the appraiser level, and on request the Assessor must provide a copy of the most recent appraisal within 15 days.

If that does not settle it, the formal steps are:

  1. Ask the Assessor for the petition form, giving the owner name and parcel number or street address.
  2. File a separate petition for each parcel, or for each parcel under different ownership, no later than January 15.
  3. Wait for written notice of the hearing date, which the county sends at least ten days ahead.
  4. Attend the hearing, which is held under Nevada's Open Meeting Law and concludes on or before February 28.

You do not need an attorney or accountant. Anyone appealing for the owner needs written authorization signed by the owner, and an attorney must be licensed before the highest court of a state.

The Board can only consider valuation. It cannot change a tax rate, and it cannot lower a value because of financial hardship. A later appeal goes to the State Board of Equalization and then the courts.

What happens to Douglas County property tax when I sell?

Unpaid property tax is paid from the sale proceeds at closing, and the title company asks the Clerk-Treasurer for the current balance. Nevada bills real property in installments, with the first due on the third Monday of August and later installments in October, January and March under NRS 361.483. Penalties of 4%, 5%, 6% and 7% apply as one to four installments go unpaid, after a ten-day grace period.

A cash sale does not change who owes what, only how fast the balance is cleared. Ask the Clerk-Treasurer for a payoff figure and have the title company put it on the settlement statement.

The recording side adds one more cost. Nevada's Real Property Transfer Tax is $1.95 for every $500 of value in every county, collected by the County Recorder when the deed is recorded. Buyer and seller are responsible together and individually, so the parties normally agree in the contract who pays. The Department of Taxation's own example puts the base tax on a $100,500 transfer at $393.90. A Declaration of Value form must accompany the deed.

The Department lists exemptions, including transfers to or from a trust without consideration and a deed upon death under NRS 111.109, which matters when heirs are selling.

Which Douglas County roads, airports and services affect a sale?

Buyers and appraisers look at access, and Douglas County has a few distinct corridors. The major highways are US 50, US 395, and State Routes 28, 88, 206, 207, 208, 756, 757, 759 and 760. Public transit options named for the county are Douglas Area Rural Transit, the Tahoe Transportation District and Eastern Sierra Transit.

The county operates the Minden-Tahoe Airport. Fire and emergency medical service comes from the Tahoe-Douglas Fire Protection District at the lake and the East Fork Fire Protection District across the rest of the county.

Nevada bills combine county, school, fire and other local levies by tax district, so two houses a few miles apart can carry different rates.

What do Douglas County sellers usually run into?

Sellers here usually face a timing problem more than a market problem. The most common situations are these:

  • An heir lives out of state, has no local contact and needs a clear payoff from the Clerk-Treasurer.
  • A house has a remodel or addition that has not been reflected on the tax roll, so the abatement does not apply and the next bill jumps.
  • An owner missed the January 15 appeal deadline and waits a full year to challenge a value.

Cash Home Buyers works with owners in these situations, buying houses as-is with no commission. A written offer is free, and you can decline it without owing anything. Confirm every deadline and figure with the Douglas County Assessor and Clerk-Treasurer before you rely on it, because dates and rates change each fiscal year.

More questions about Douglas County, NV Property Tax Guide

Who bills property tax in Douglas County, Nevada?

The Douglas County Clerk-Treasurer bills and collects the tax, and the Assessor values the property. Douglas County has no incorporated cities, so one pair of offices serves every community from Gardnerville to Stateline.

What is the deadline to appeal a Douglas County property assessment?

January 15, filed with the Assessor's office. Hearings before the County Board of Equalization are scheduled as needed and concluded on or before February 28, with at least ten days written notice.

Can the Board of Equalization lower my value because I cannot afford the tax?

No. The county says the Boards can only consider valuation, not tax rates or taxes, and cannot reduce a valuation because of financial hardship.

Is there a cap on how much my Douglas County property tax can rise?

Yes, for most property. Owner-occupied single-family primary residences are limited to a 3% increase, and other property falls under a general abatement of up to 8%. The caps do not apply to new improvements or a change in use.

How much is the transfer tax when I sell a house in Douglas County?

The statewide base rate is $1.95 for every $500 of value, collected by the County Recorder when the deed is recorded. The Department of Taxation says buyer and seller share responsibility for it, so the contract should say who pays.

Can I sell a Douglas County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. The balance is paid from the proceeds at closing, and the title company gets the payoff from the Clerk-Treasurer. Penalties keep growing until it is paid, so a faster closing helps.
